newsitem.title: MEXICO: Tension as Mexico rebels prepare to leave jungle.
newsitem.headline: Tension as Mexico rebels prepare to leave jungle.
newsitem.dateline: SAN CRISTOBAL DE LAS CASAS, Mexico 1996-10-07

text.p: A group of left-wing Mexicans left for the jungle on Monday to meet Zapatista leaders on a mission that has presented a tricky challenge to President Ernesto Zedillo.

The group around 100 people intends to escort a group of top rebel commanders by road on their first-ever trip outside their southern base state of Chiapas to Mexico City to attend a forum on Indian rights.
The proposed journey by men who led a violent rebellion against the government in Chiapas in January 1994, causing around 145 deaths, comes at an awkward time for the government.

Peace talks with the Zapatistas, which have dragged on for over a year, were suspended in early September after the rebels accused the government of acting in bad faith and show no sign of restarting any time soon.
Chief government negotiator Marco Antonio Bernal has warned the rebels they risk arrest if they attempt any trip outside the state before a final peace treaty is signed.

The rebels, aware of the enormous publicity they would gain from a three or four day road journey through southern Mexico watched by international media, appear to be weighing whether the government will risk a violent response in front of cameras if they try to break out of Chiapas.
The Zapatistas were to take a final decision about the journey late on Monday when the commission reached their strongholds in the Lacandon jungle near the border with Guatemala.

The escort group left the colonial Chipas city of San Cristobal de las Casas, 370 miles (600 km) southeast of Mexico City, on Monday for a seven-hour journey on poor roads to the hamlet of La Realidad on the edge of the jungle.

Attempting last-minute talks to head off a possible clash, members of COCOPA, an all-party legislative commission which has mediated peace talks in Chiapas, flew by helicopter to La Realidad to meet Zapatista leaders.

Referring to fears of fresh fighting in Chiapas if the armed rebels move out of the jungle, top Zapatista spokesman Javier Elorriaga told reporters that "the Zapatistas will come out (of the jungle) in a signal of peace, not of war".
Elorriaga said he took it for granted that a group of top rebels would come to Mexico City, possibly including the charismatic Zapatista leader Subcommander Marcos.

"I don't know how many will come, the invitation is open and we wouldn't rule out Marcos himself," he told reporters. "There is no law that prohibits the Zapatistas from moving through the territory of their country".
Reporters who travelled part of the way along the roads between San Cristobal and La Realidad said troops in the area had been reinforced and had stepped up checks on travellers.
Military chiefs in Chiapas denied this, saying they had orders not to interfere with the commission's journey to La Realidad.
